To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the addition of maize gluten meal to a high-energy diet containing 8% wheat and 12% barley, and 12.25% maize gluten meal, resulted in an increase in egg production and egg mass of 5.6% and 5.9%, respectively, over the high-energy control.

the inclusion of maize gluten meal in high energy diets for laying hens is feasible without the use of protein supplements, and that the use of L-lys-HCl and DL-met in the diets with 12.25% maize gluten meal increased the egg production, feed conversion and egg quality.

(1) the use of a high energy diet in the present experiment resulted in a high egg production and egg mass; (2) the use of maize gluten meal in the high energy diet resulted in a lower egg production and egg quality than the high energy diet containing fish meal; (3) the use of L-lys-HCl and DL-met in the maize gluten meal diets improved egg quality and production, but not egg mass, compared with diets without these amino acids.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of high-energy, low-cost diets for poultry, based on the use of maize gluten meal (MGM) as the sole protein source.
the use of maize gluten meal in high energy diets for laying hens.
the development of a new type of high energy diet for caged layers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of maize gluten meal, with or without the addition of lysine or methionine, as a protein source, in diets for caged layers, is not recommended.

the addition of maize gluten meal to a high energy diet based on wheat, barley and soya bean meal, with or without supplementation with L-lysine or L-lysinoe and DL-methione, does not affect performance in laying hens.

the addition of L-lysHCl to the diet containing maize gluten meal at 8.25% and the addition of DL-methionne with L-lysine to the diets containing 12.25% and 15.75% maize gluten meal, significantly improved performance of the hens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

maize gluten meal is a suitable protein source for laying hens, but that it is inferior to white fish meal in its protein quality and that it should be used at the lower levels in the range 12-15% in diets containing 8-12% crude protein.
the addition of L-lysHCl to the maize gluten diets increased egg production, egg weight and feed intake and improved the efficiency of egg production and feed conversion ratio.

the addition of maize gluten meal, with and without supplements, to cereal-based high energy layer diets can be used to provide the protein requirements of laying hens without any adverse effect on production performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

maize gluten meal can be fed as a source of supplementary protein at levels of up to 15.25% in cereal-based high-energy diets for caged layers, provided the diet contains adequate levels of lysine and methionine.
we have developed a method that allows for the production of a large number of protein -based nanoparticles with tunable properties.

the addition of 2.5% maize gluten meal (as a replacement for 2.5 % white fish meal) to a high energy diet for egg-laying pullets and hens is beneficial in terms of egg production, egg quality and feed conversion efficiency, but that the addition of maize gluten meal beyond 2.5 percent is not justified.
